https://www.baltictimes.com/europe_wants.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Europe wants everything. The question Is what comes first 2026-07-20 Vidmantas Janulevicius Photo: Vidmantas Janulevicius is the President of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists (LPK), Chairman of the Board, BOD GROUP Europe does not suffer from a lack of ambition. If anything, it may be suffering from the opposite. The continent wants to strengthen its defence capabilities after decades of underinvestment. It wants to accelerate the green transition while reducing dependence on imported energy. It wants to compete with the United States and China in artificial intelligence and advanced technologies. It wants to preserve its social model despite ageing populations and growing fiscal pressures. And it wants to remain globally competitive in a world that is becoming less open, less predictable and more geopolitical. Each of these goals is rational. The question is whether Europe can realistically pursue all of them at the same speed. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, this question has become more urgent. NATO's commitment to move towards defence spending equivalent to 5% of GDP reflects a strategic reality that Europe can no longer ignore. Security has returned to the centre of political and economic decision-making. Yet the debate about defence increasingly risks focusing on the wrong problem. Across Europe, discussions revolve around where additional money should come from, how much governments can borrow, which taxes should be raised or which expenditures should be reduced. These are legitimate questions, but they overlook a more fundamental one. What if Europe's biggest constraint is not fiscal capacity, but competitive capacity? And what if the scarcest strategic resource of the next decade is not money, energy or even critical minerals, but Europe's ability to innovate? The real challenge facing Europe is not simply how to finance its ambitions. It is how to sustain them. A continent with weak productivity growth, high energy costs, ageing demographics and declining industrial competitiveness will eventually struggle to finance any long-term strategy, regardless of how ambitious its targets may be. For years, Europe benefited from conditions that allowed it to postpone difficult choices. Globalisation expanded markets. Cheap energy lowered costs. Stable geopolitical conditions reduced security concerns. Growth was often sufficient to accommodate competing priorities. That environment no longer exists. Europe is trying to rearm, decarbonise, digitalise and preserve its welfare model at the same time, while growing more slowly than its principal competitors. At precisely the moment when Europe is being asked to spend more on defence, it is also facing stronger competition from both the United States and China. Washington has embraced industrial policy on a scale that would have seemed unlikely only a decade ago. Beijing continues to strengthen its manufacturing position through long-term planning, state-backed financing and strategic control of critical supply chains. Europe, meanwhile, has been reluctant to acknowledge that pursuing every objective comes with trade-offs. This is not primarily a defence problem. It is a prioritisation problem. For smaller, export-oriented economies such as those of the Baltic States, the consequences of getting this balance wrong may become visible sooner than elsewhere. The answer will depend not only on how much Europe spends, but on how much value it creates. This is why innovation deserves a far more central place in Europe's strategic thinking. Europe frequently discusses access to critical raw materials, rare earth elements, energy resources and strategic supply chains. These concerns are justified. Yet one strategic resource receives far less attention despite becoming increasingly important for both competitiveness and security. Innovation. Europe cannot quickly reverse demographic trends. It cannot easily replicate the scale of American capital markets. Nor is it likely to enjoy the same energy-cost advantages as some of its competitors. Innovation is one of the few resources that can expand despite those constraints. In the coming decade, the ability to generate, commercialise and scale new ideas may become as strategically important as access to energy, capital or critical minerals. For countries such as Lithuania, competing through scale alone will always be difficult. We can, however, compete through knowledge, technology and innovation. The challenge is no longer producing good ideas. It is creating an environment in which those ideas can become globally competitive businesses. Europe's defence debate is therefore becoming something much larger than a discussion about military spending. It is becoming a debate about competitiveness. And Europe's competitiveness debate is increasingly becoming a debate about innovation. Ultimately, Europe's future will not be determined by how many strategies it adopts or how many targets it announces. It will be determined by whether it can make difficult choices, establish clear priorities and create the economic capacity needed to support its ambitions. Because security, like prosperity, cannot be financed indefinitely through borrowing, redistribution or taxation alone. In the coming decade, Europe will need many things: more security, more resilience and more investment. But above all, it will need a resource that receives far less attention than defence budgets, energy imports or critical minerals. It will need more innovation. Because in an increasingly competitive world, innovation is becoming not only an economic asset, but a strategic one. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-close.text: BRUSSELS — The EU is looking to Israel to support its new push for high-tech air defense and space capabilities. Israel Space Agency boss Shimrit Maman this week traveled to Brussels where she met Tuesday with Ekaterina Zaharieva, European commissioner for startups, research and innovation for talks on key areas like AI and robotics. The visit comes before Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her first major speech on space at a summit in Paris on Thursday, where she is expected to warn of growing hostilities and the need for Europe to step up its presence in space. Advertisement Advertisement "It's very hard to do things on your own," Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space "is already happening — we just don't realize how much" and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in "dual-use" technology for both civilian and defense purposes. "One of the things we are working on is early warning systems," she said. "We saw that very nicely in the last round [of missile strikes] we had with Iran, for example. How we are managing to get [warnings to] all the civilians in Israel and not have that many casualties. That's part of that system. We are working on that very wide look that you're able to warn in advance, have that system warn the citizens." A string of recent deals have seen the EU pursue closer military and technological relations with Israel, after several years of effective disengagement as a result of political tensions that have followed the war in Gaza. However, competition from Washington and strategic rivalries with Moscow and Beijing have created a need for allies with advanced industrial capabilities. In 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed calls from Polish and Greek Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Kyriakos Mitsotakis to create an EU-funded air defense shield . However, three senior officials involved in the discussions told POLITICO the plans did not move ahead after the Commission and a handful of capitals concluded it would need to rely on Israeli air-defense technology, which they deemed too sensitive a year into the Gaza conflict. Now though, in a major expansion of its operations in Europe, Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems confirmed Monday that it will open a factory producing its Iron Dome air-defense system in a former Volkswagen factory in Germany. One week ago, Greece struck a €3 billion deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to build a new multilayered air defense network designed to take down drones, hostile jets and rockets. Advertisement Advertisement "We see that convergence of everything, of that multi-layer defense approach," said Maman, pointing to satellite imaging and AI modeling as a key focus for joint development. "I don't treat only defense as ballistic missiles from Iran ... think about a fire or a flash flood or even a prolonged drought ... we have a proven track record and we do have very good results," she said. Antoaneta Roussi, Jordyn Dahl, Chris Lunday and Romanus Otte contributed to this report.

Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty Images Assisted dying MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales Bill fails at second reading despite near-identical legislation being approved by Commons in last parliament UK politics live – latest updates Peter Walker Senior political correspondent Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.36 EDT First published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A bill to permit assisted dying in England and Wales has been voted down by MPs, almost certainly stopping such a measure from being enacted before the next general election at the very least least. In the second reading of the bill, put forward by Labour’s Lauren Edwards, MPs voted by 286 to 270 for it to be blocked. The result is a reversal of MPs’ support for a near-identical version of the bill, which sought to allow adults with terminal illnesses and less than six months to live to end their lives with the approval of a panel of experts. This was approved by the Commons in the last parliament. While some MPs cheered and hugged in the Commons chamber after Friday’s result, the scuppering of the idea caused significant anger among supporters of assisted dying, who believe the measure should already have become law. The previous bill, sponsored by another Labour MP, Kim Leadbeater, passed through the Commons but was blocked in the Lords , where it was talked out by a handful of peers who tabled a huge number of amendments. 4:36 MPs recount personal experiences as they debate assisted dying bill – video In a statement after the vote, Edwards said the public broadly supported a change in the law and “will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it and MPs balked at insisting that they do their job”. She added: “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.” On its second reading, Leadbeater’s bill was approved by 330 votes to 275, and by 313 to 291 at the third reading. The fact that the vote tally for both sides dropped in Friday’s result – with that of the pro side falling more – suggests it was sunk as much by a lack of enthusiasm than by MPs changing side. Some MPs had said they were lobbied by pro-assisted dying campaigners notably less this time than with Leadbeater’s bill. As the issue is deemed a matter of conscience, it had been left to a private member’s bill rather than a government-sponsored one, with Andy Burnham and his ministers staying officially neutral. However, the prime minister has been seen as less supportive than Keir Starmer, by announcing he would not vote on the bill – his predecessor voted in favour – and saying he believed the debate on assisted dying should be paused until social care was improved. Closing a sometimes emotional debate on Friday, the health minister Alison McGovern said the government would enact the plan if it became law, but reiterated concerns about social care. She said: “In my opinion, social care has been ignored for far too long, both the 1.5 million people, mainly women, who work in it, and the families who need it, and we heard that across the house today.” Opening the debate, Edwards said it was a false choice to say the issue should be delayed ahead of improvements in social and palliative care. She said: “We must grasp that opportunity in front of us to create a holistic end of life care system that will deliver choice and dignity for every single one of our constituents.” During the debate, the Labour MP Claire Hazelgrove, who supported the bill, said her mother chose to end her life aged 61 while suffering a late-stage terminal illness. Hazelgrove said: “She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated. I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.” Another Labour MP, Ashley Dalton, who has been diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer , said the assisted dying bill did not adequately protect people with treatable depression who also had a terminal illness. https://www.liverpoolecho.co.uk/whats-on.text: Liz Earle enthusiasts have been rushing to get their hands on a set that delivers almost £125 worth of free skin and bodycare . The British botanical brand has unveiled their festive countdowns for 2026, marking some of their most substantial savings of the year. Last month, Liz Earle introduced not one, but two beauty advent calendars in advance of the holiday season. The 24-day calendar, which was priced at £175, has already completely sold out, but devotees of the brand can still secure considerable savings and a glut of products for a fraction of the cost with their 12 Days of Liz Earle Beauty Advent Calendar. Equally impressive yet more budget-friendly, the 12 Days of Liz Earle Beauty Advent Calendar is priced at £79, yet contains £203.50 worth of Liz Earle products. That means shoppers are receiving £124.50 worth of products for free. As part of the offer, each item (excluding the cloth) works out at £6.59, which is rather impressive considering one of the products is worth £67.50 on its own, reports the Express .. The standout item is undoubtedly the Superskin Moisturiser with Natural Neroli 75ml, which usually costs £11.50 less than the entire £79 calendar. Formulated to diminish the visibility of fine lines and wrinkles, it contains pomegranate flower extract combined with cranberry, rosehip and British borage seed oils, which collaborate to seal in hydration and leave complexions appearing fuller and more refined. The collection also features a 100ml bottle of the brand's popular, award-winning Cleanse & Polish Hot Cloth Cleanser , alongside a compact Instant Boost Skin Tonic and Eyebright Soothing Eye Lotion. However, the calendar doesn't just feature facial skincare. Purchasers can also discover a Botanical Body Wash, Botanical Body Cream and Hand Cream in a limited edition Mandarin & Nutmeg scent, which can't be found elsewhere at present. It's also gaining traction amongst customers, with one reviewer calling the festive fragrance 'divine'. One customer who purchased the countdown said: "Attractive packaging. Good value. When you open the box the smell was divine," while another added: "So worth the money. Such an amazing Christmas gift." A third customer commented: "This is a lovely set of Liz Earle products for a fantastic price. I especially love the new Christmas Mandarin and Nutmeg fragrance as it is subtle and not overpowering as I have already opened the contents. I couldn't wait. Value is excellent and this calendar a great way to try some other products if you haven't already." However, as is frequently the case with advent calendars or beauty boxes, there's a possibility that some customers may not appreciate every single item inside, or discover that the occasional product doesn't suit their skin type. Some may not be keen on the fragrance, while others might simply prefer a countdown offering a wider range of brands or more diverse products. One such option is the OK! Beauty Box Advent Calendar, which has completely sold out three years running. Developed in partnership with MUA Hannah Martin, it contains 25 products - 22 of which are full-size. Priced at £109 but valued at over £605, it's brimming with makeup, skincare, fragrance, haircare, nail care, wellbeing products and beauty tools. Customers can look forward to brands including Bobbi Brown, bareMinerals, Kosas and Weleda, alongside everything from a travel brush set to a luxury eye cream worth more than £145. Meanwhile, a more budget-friendly option is the Macmillan 24 Doors Of Joy Beauty Advent Calendar, which is presently on offer at Boots, reduced to £44 from £90 . It features products from brands such as Liz Earle and No7, as well as Champneys and Soap and Glory — ideal for some indulgent pampering. It's always worth examining the full contents of an advent calendar prior to purchasing, to ensure you'll make use of the majority of items. Photograph: LM Otero/AP View image in fullscreen McKenna West, left, arrivers with her legal team for a court hearing in Dallas in August. Photograph: LM Otero/AP Texas Baby born via surrogate can leave Texas for treatment in California, court rules Ruling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate rejected couple’s request for abortion Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.46 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Texas supreme court has decided that the month-old infant that surrogate McKenna West gave birth to can be relocated to Los Angeles, a Thursday ruling that came weeks after a California court had recognized the biological parents’ custody rights. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the court wrote in a Thursday order, referring to the baby’s rare severe heart defect. West had attempted to block the biological parents from removing the child from Texas and taking him to a hospital in Los Angeles where the couple live. The court cited testimony from the infant’s Texas physician, who described the window for an ICU-to-ICU transfer as short and “ripe now”. West’s attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Thursday ruling. The infant, named Rumi by his biological parents, has hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery. Without treatment, the defect can be fatal. The condition was detected when the baby was a fetus, prompting California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed to ask that West terminate the pregnancy. West, who resides in Alaska, traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to deliver the child. West and her legal team maintain that the couple attempted to force her into having the procedure, while lawyers for Gilkar and Ahmed say that West initially agreed to the abortion, before blindsiding them with the legal battle for custody. The case has stoked enormous debate around abortion and parental rights, particularly in conservative mediasphere. Texas attorney general Ken Paxton elevated the dispute’s national profile, when he intervened to ensure the baby would receive medical care after his birth. West had appealed to the US supreme court, suggesting Gilkar and Ahmed would put the baby into end-of-life care at a hospice rather than continue treatment for the heart defect. West was seeking to be informed about the baby’s medical status and to “advocate for her rights,” according to court documents. “Ordinarily, MW would have been deemed [the baby’s] mother under Texas law by virtue of giving birth to him. But because of the unlawful California judgment, she has been dismissed with prejudice from the Texas proceedings and denied any information,” West’s lawyers wrote in a court filing, using West’s initials. The couple’s attorneys responded in a court filing saying “there is simply no truth whatsoever” to the hospice claim. They argued that if the court sided with West it would sow confusion over who had authority to dictate and consent to medical decisions for the child. Gilkar told a Dallas court in August that Rumi was “the most beautiful person”. “He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot,” she said. Photograph: AIS60/Getty Images/iStockphoto View image in fullscreen Paphos, Cyprus, near where the incident occurred. Photograph: AIS60/Getty Images/iStockphoto Cyprus Briton due to face Cypriot court after tragic death of two-year-old son Human rights lawyer says accused father is victim of ‘archaic system’ after boy fell from window in July Helena Smith in Nicosia Tue 22 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 04.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British father is expected to appear in court in Cyprus accused of “recklessly” causing the death of his two-year-old son, who was fatally injured falling from a fourth-floor window. The 37-year-old, who has not been named publicly, was on the first day of a family holiday near Paphos on 12 July when the toddler died. At 9am on Tuesday, 10 weeks after his son’s death, the distraught City executive will appear before the resort town’s district court to answer a charge that until last week he hoped would be suspended. “My client’s disappointment is obvious,” his lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters after the island’s top legal official rejected an appeal to discontinue the procedure on humanitarian grounds. “He is not in a good way.” A desperate plea for George Savvides, the attorney general of Cyprus, to intervene was the last hope of a reprieve for a family still reeling from the “unimaginable loss”. “In these exceptional circumstances, we do not believe a continued criminal process serves the public interest,” said Alexandrou. “The focus now should be on [the family’s] welfare and recovery.” The toddler’s father was inconsolable when he appeared in the same courtroom to be formally charged in July. After posting €30,000 (£26,100) in bail to return to the UK to attend the toddler’s funeral in August, the father was forced under threat of extradition to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September. In a move that has stirred further debate over the way Cypriot authorities have handled the case, state prosecutors, addressing Paphos’ district court last week, said while Savvides recognised the father’s grief, it was a matter of “public interest” that the criminal proceedings went ahead. If convicted, the defendant, described as a banker at one of the big four accountancy firms, faces a maximum sentence of four years in prison. He now confronts the agonising choice of either pleading not guilty – which will open the way to a trial expected to last months – or entering a guilty plea in the hope that the court will take mitigating circumstances into account at sentencing. In the event of a criminal trial, there could be weeks of high drama at a time when he was still mourning the loss of his son, his lawyer said, adding: “I will have to sit down, explain the procedure, explain where we stand today and what the pros and cons are.” On the eve of the plea hearing, it remained unknown how the defendant would contest the charge of causing his son’s demise “through negligent, reckless or dangerous actions”. The boy, who would have turned three last week, fell from the fourth-floor window at the King Evelthon hotel and resort on the Chlorakas coastline outside Paphos. The father claims he placed him on the windowsill, – along a corridor leading to a lift that his relatives were about to use – not realising the window was ajar. The toddler then fell backwards, suffering fatal cranial injuries when he hit a veranda 10 metres (33ft) below. In a nation so dependent on tourism, criticism has mounted as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats have questioned the perceived lack of compassion with which officials have approached the case. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion While the letter of the law had been adhered to so assiduously by police and court officials, “no one had asked why the window did not have bars”, said a diplomat based in Nicosia, the eastern Mediterranean island’s capital. “It’s perplexing that there’s all this emphasis on the father being a criminal and so little focus on the circumstances in which the boy died,” he added. “Why was there even a window there and why was it open? In a country where permits to build hotels are often lax, these are questions that should not be ignored.” In an editorial last week, the Cyprus Mail echoed that sentiment. “Why are authorities so eager to treat tragic accidents as criminal acts?” it asked, after a similar incident in which the three-year-old son of African immigrants fell to his death from the balcony of his family’s sixth-floor apartment in Nicosia. Like the Briton, his parents were held in custody for several days although they were eventually released without charge. With the prospect of prolonged criminal proceedings in store for the Essex-born executive, debate has intensified over the role of Cyprus’ attorney general, long regarded as one of the most controversial legacies of the island’s former status as a British colony. In his ninth-floor office in the heart of Nicosia, the island’s leading human rights lawyer, Achilleas Demetriades, said the Briton had fallen foul of “an archaic system” that was long overdue an overhaul. Under Cyprus’s post-colonial justice system, such decisions remained entirely at the discretion of the attorney general, he said, and could not be challenged. “Sadly, this man has fallen victim to an archaic system in which one man, the attorney general, has unfettered power which is finally under review,” said Demetriades, a candidate in the last presidential elections. “This certainly raises human rights issues.” Explore more on these topics Cyprus Europe Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Salam Ahmadyan (left) and Rahman Salehi are alleged to have carried out ‘hostile reconnaissance’ within Manchester’s Jewish community. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA View image in fullscreen Salam Ahmadyan (left) and Rahman Salehi are alleged to have carried out ‘hostile reconnaissance’ within Manchester’s Jewish community. Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PA UK news Two Iranian men identified Manchester synagogue as site for alleged bomb plot, court hears Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, were charged with preparing attacks on city’s Jewish community, including Heaton Park synagogue Sammy Gecsoyler Sat 3 Oct 2026 08.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two Iranian men identified a Manchester synagogue previously subjected to a fatal terrorist attack as a target for an alleged homemade bomb plot, a court has heard. Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool were charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism on Friday. The two men appeared in Westminster magistrates court on Saturday morning. They wore grey overalls in the dock while and, through a Kurdish interpreter, spoke to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses. The pair were alleged to have carried out “hostile reconnaissance” within Manchester’s Jewish community and identified a number of potential targets including the city’s Jewish museum and Heaton Park synagogue. The court heard the pair came to the UK illegally via small boats. Salehi arrived in 2020 before being granted leave to remain in 2023. Ahmadyan came in 2023 and has an outstanding asylum claim. They were in contact with a third party, believed to be operating from within Iran, who “directed and coordinated” the planned attack and sent them “instructions on how to prepare an explosive device”. Prosecutor Mark Luckett told the court: “Both defendants are accused of preparing acts of terrorism targeting the Jewish community in Manchester through the use of a homemade explosive device. “The defendants were observed carrying out, what the prosecution say, is a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community, identifying attempted targets such as the Jewish Museum and Heaton Park synagogue.” “They were in contact with a third party who is alleged to have directed and coordinated the planned attack and provided instructions on how to assemble a homemade explosive device,” he said. “It is assessed this individual is also an Iranian national and most likely operating from within Iran.” The two men were arrested on 20 September 2026 in broad daylight, just before the festival of Yom Kippur, widely regarded as the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. Before coming to the UK, Salehi lived in Germany for five years. The men are accused of acquiring a document entitled Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb and video material on how to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of acquiring liquids, components and equipment required in order to manufacture or assemble an improvised explosive device. They are also accused of using the internet to identify and research potential targets, acquiring images, plans and maps of potential targets and conducting reconnaissance of potential locations for attack. District judge Nina Tempia remanded the two men into custody to appear at the Old Bailey on 23 October Explore more on these topics UK news news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
